Q: Why does clang use fsub.4s for a single scalar subtraction? How can I prevent this? A:

One way to prevent it, though you may not like it overall: compile with -ftrapping-math. Try on godbolt

This option tells the compiler that floating point exceptions could trap (even if that's not actually true at runtime; AFAIK Apple CPUs don't support it). If so, then subtracting the high elements of the vectors could result in a trap that should not have occurred if only the requested subtraction had been done, and so the compiler isn't allowed to do it.

Note that -ftrapping-math is documented as being enabled by default with GCC, but evidently not for Clang. (But turning it off still does not make GCC emit vector fsub for this code.)

Of course, it's very possible that -ftrapping-math suppresses other optimizations that you actually wanted. For instance, if you were subtracting three of the four elements, you would probably rather do a single vector subtraction, even if you don't need the top element. But -ftrapping-math forces it to be done as three scalar subtractions.

Q: What is the purpose of std::meta::variable_of? A:

A reflection produced by std::meta::parameters_of doesn't really represent a parameter (as introduced by a parameter declaration). It conceptually represents "a position in a function's parameter list".

Compare this reflection with the result of applying ^^ to a parameter name. Only the latter represents the variable introduced by the parameter declaration.

This distinction is evident when a function is redeclared:

void f([[=1]] int a);
void f([[=2]] const int b);

Here a and b are different variables. They have different types, different names, and different annotations.

Note that these parameters are different variables even if they have the same name and type, because they belong to different function parameter scopes.

A reflection of b would only tell information about b:

  • identifier_of returns "b".
  • type_of returns ^^const int.
  • annotations_of returns a vector containing only a reflection of [[=2]].

A reflection produced by parameters_of(^^f)[0], conversely, would consider all declarations of f:

  • identifier_of throws because has_identifier returns false, because the declarations are inconsistent regarding the parameter name.
  • type_of returns ^^int, the type of the first parameter in the type of f.
  • annotations_of returns a vector containing a reflection of [[=1]] followed by a reflection of [[=2]].

The purpose of std::meta::variable_of is very specific: it converts a reflection produced by parameters_of(^^f) to one produced by ^^ in the context of f's definition.

IMO, the confusing is due to the standard describing a reflection produced by parameters_of as representing a function parameter. As illustrated above, such a reflection represents a position and not a concrete parameter. It is kind of similar to a reflection produced by bases_of, which represents an element in the base clause (formally, a direct base class relationship) rather than a class.

Q: Why is Gatherer not marked as a functional interface? A:

having only one abstract method doesn't automatically mean an interface should be marked @FunctionalInterface. The annotation is mainly a design intention that says the interface is meant to be used as a function/lambda. Gatherer.Integrator represents a specific piece of behavior, so it makes sense as a functional interface, while Gatherer represents a complete gathering operation with multiple pieces of behavior. So although Gatherer technically qualifies, it's not intended to be used as a lambda itself.

Q: What is a proper way to handle a constructor process that might fail? A:

A constructor that fails should throw an exception.

The exception should be handled somewhere. Not necessarily at the place where the instance is constructed, this is not always the most appropriate place. It should be handled like any other exception. There is nothing special about it being a construction failure.

The point of exceptions is to free the programmer from the obligation to check error codes at every call site, and handle failures in a centralized way. For example, if your operation is to copy a file, it might contain several sub-operation like opening the source file, opening the destination file, reading, and writing. You should not catch exceptions right where each individual sub-operation is invoked. Rather, wrap your top-level operation in a try-catch block.

Q: How to suppress phpseclib "Invalid HMAC" warning A:

The "Invalid HMAC" is not a warning, it's a fatal error. You cannot suppress it.

The error indicates there's some misunderstanding in communication between the server and the phpseclib client.

The error has nothing to do with the "host key verification". Contrary to majority of SSH clients, the phpseclib does not actually even verify the host key. You have code this yourself.

See https://phpseclib.com/docs/ssh2/connect#basic-example-with-signature-verification

(but again, this has nothing to do with the error you are getting)

Q: SFTP in PHP with Key A:

The code you are trying is for old version of phpseclib.

In the latest version, use:

$key = PublicKeyLoader::load(file_get_contents('/path/to/privatekey.pem'));

See https://phpseclib.com/docs/publickeys/overview#loading-keys
